title: Travel and farewells
goal: Handle a trip on your own — airport, hotel, directions — and close twenty units by gathering up everything you now have.
bekal: handle departure, lodging and the unexpected on a trip

dialogs.title: Dialogue — Lennujaamas
dialogs.intro: Late June, Tallinn Airport. Budi's exchange semester is over. Kerli sees him off.

lines.speaker: Kerli:
lines.text: Kas sul on kõik olemas? Pass, pilet, telefon?
lines.id: Do you have everything? Passport, ticket, phone?
lines.literal: question you-at is everything there? passport, ticket, phone?

lines.speaker: Kerli:
lines.id: Good. What time does your flight leave?

lines.speaker: Kerli:
lines.text: Sul on veel aega. Kas sa jood midagi?
lines.id: There's still time. Want something to drink?
lines.literal: you-at is still time-part. question you drink-you something?

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.id: One coffee. My last one in Estonia.

lines.speaker: Kerli:
lines.text: Ära ütle nii. Sa tuled tagasi.
lines.id: Don't say that. You'll be back.
lines.literal: don't say so. you come-you back.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Ma loodan. Ma tahaksin siin magistrit teha.
lines.id: I hope so. I'd like to do my master's here.
lines.literal: I hope-I. I want-would-I here master-part to-make.

lines.speaker: Kerli:
lines.text: Siis pead sa eesti keelt edasi õppima.
lines.id: Then you have to keep studying Estonian.
lines.literal: then must-you you Estonian language-part further to-study.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Ma tean. Aga vaata — me räägime praegu eesti keeles.
lines.id: I know. But look — we're speaking Estonian right now.
lines.literal: I know-I. but look — we speak-we now Estonian language-in.

lines.speaker: Kerli:
lines.id: All morning. I didn't even notice.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.id: In January I couldn't even say "tere".

lines.speaker: Kerli:
lines.text: Ja nüüd sa vaidled minuga vältevahelduse üle.
lines.id: And now you're arguing with me about vowel length.
lines.literal: and now you argue-you me-with length-change-gen about.

lines.speaker: Kerli:
lines.text: Aga sa pidasid vastu. Sellel on rohkem väärtust.
lines.id: But you kept at it. That's worth more.
lines.literal: but you endured-you against. that-at is more value-part.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.id: Thank you for everything, Kerli. Really.

lines.speaker: Kerli:
lines.text: Pole tänu väärt. Head reisi ja nägemiseni!
lines.id: Don't mention it. Have a good trip, and see you soon!
lines.literal: not-is thanks worth. good-gen trip-part and see-you-soon!

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Nägemiseni. Ma tulen tagasi — sel korral talveks.
lines.id: See you. I'll be back — this time for the winter.
lines.literal: see-you. I come-I back — this time-in winter-for.

notes: **Nägemiseni** is warmer than *nägemist* — literally "until seeing again", with the ending *-ni* (until) from unit 8. For a farewell that really matters, this is the word.
**Pole tänu väärt** — "not worth thanks". One of the most natural replies to *aitäh*, a partner to *palun* which you've known since unit 1.

**Ma ei märganudki** — notice the ending **-ki/-gi** meaning "even, also": *ma ei teadnudki* (I didn't even know), *keegi ei tulnudki* (nobody came at all). It attaches to the end of the word and adds emphasis.
**Talveks** = *talv* + **-ks**, "for the winter". This ending expresses purpose or change: *kingituseks* (as a gift), *õhtuks* (by evening), *läheb külmaks* (it's getting cold — from unit 18).

grammars.title: At the airport, station and hotel
body: These twenty sentences cover almost all travel business at A1.

head: Eesti keel
English
rows: What time does the flight leave?
I'd like a room for two nights.

after: ⚠️ *Kaheks ööks* uses the ending **-ks** twice — on the number and on the noun. Same pattern: *kolmeks päevaks* (for three days), *nädalaks* (for a week).
*Broneering* (reservation) and *registreerimine* (registration, check-in) are two long words that match English through the same European roots — compare "reservation" and "registration".

grammars.title: Parting — choosing the right one
body: Estonian has several ways to say goodbye, and the choice depends on how long you'll be apart.

head: Eesti keel
Literal
When to use it
rows: Warmer, for a goodbye that matters.
A warm farewell, often for good.

after: ⚠️ *Head ööd* isn't an ordinary goodbye — it's used only when parting to go to sleep, as warned in unit 1.
If you remember only one, remember **nägemist**. It's right in almost every situation and never sounds wrong.

blocks.text: You're now at the end of A1. That means you can handle yourself in Estonian for everyday business: introducing yourself, shopping, ordering, asking directions, making plans, telling about yesterday, and declining politely. That's not a small thing.

What awaits at A2 is roughly this: **the full plural** (this module deliberately held it back), **perfect and pluperfect tenses** treated fully, **complex sentences** with *et*, *kui*, *sest*, and **particle verbs** — *ära*, *läbi*, *kinni*, *lahti* — that change a verb's meaning completely. Plus three to four thousand words.

blocks.title: Four things that really speed you up
items: **Listen more than you read.** The third vowel length is never written. The radio stations *Vikerraadio* and *ERR* are free and speak at a normal speed.
**Write new words as pairs.** *jalg – jala*, *sööma – süüa*. This habit is the single most time-saving piece of advice in the whole module.

**Speak sooner than feels comfortable.** Estonians will switch to English the moment they hear an accent. One sentence — *ma õpin eesti keelt, palun rääkige eesti keeles* — almost always makes them stay.

**Accept that you'll get the endings wrong for years.** Estonian word endings are the last thing to settle, even for people who've lived there ten years. They never block understanding. Speak wrongly, and keep speaking.

blocks.text: One last sentence, and it isn't a grammar sentence. Estonian is spoken by about one million people, and every one of them knows exactly how small that number is. That's why a foreigner who struggles to learn it is welcomed with a warmth you won't find when learning a big language. You've done the hard part. *Edu!*
